businessModel: Designer and manufacturer of specialized industrial equipment (engineered-to-order machinery plus a recurring aftermarket parts/service stream), sold B2B to industrial and infrastructure customers
businessStage: Mature, profitable, founder-owned (single majority owner) seeking a personal exit/liquidity event
sourceNote: Blind-outcome case designed to test forward-looking strategic decision quality at an ownership-transition fork. The founder must choose an exit path among three viable options. Scoring assesses whether the engine's reasoning is sound given only what is knowable at decision time; the actual outcome (which path was chosen and how it resolved) is withheld from this input and recorded only in the answer key for reference. Figures are realistic and representative.

ownerIntake.businessType: Privately held industrial equipment manufacturer, founded 1994, single founder-owner holds ~100% equity. ~$85M revenue: ~70% engineered-to-order machinery, ~30% aftermarket parts and service. ~310 employees across one main plant and two satellite service depots. ~40-year reputation, long-tenured engineering and sales relationships.
ownerIntake.stage: Revenue $85M, roughly flat-to-low-single-digit growth (mature). EBITDA ~$11M (13% margin). Aftermarket carries higher margin (~28% gross) than new machinery (~21% gross). Net debt modest (~$8M). Order backlog ~7 months. Customer concentration: top 5 customers ~38% of revenue.
ownerIntake.ownerGoal: Achieve a liquidity event that fairly values the business, protects the workforce and 40-year reputation, and lets the 64-year-old founder transition out of day-to-day leadership within ~18-24 months; choose between selling to a financial buyer, selling to a strategic buyer, or retaining ownership and running for cash flow.
ownerConstraints: Owner-availability constraint: Founder will not commit to an earn-out or operating role beyond ~24 months; any path depending on his continued daily leadership past that is unacceptable.

Workforce/reputation constraint: Founder places high weight on protecting the ~310 employees and the brand; an outcome that gutted the workforce or relocated the plant would be heavily discounted even at a higher price.
Succession constraint: There is no ready internal CEO successor; senior engineering and key customer relationships are concentrated in the founder and 2-3 long-tenured leaders.

Valuation/clean-books constraint: Financials are reliable but not audited to PE/strategic diligence standard; quality-of-earnings, customer-contract documentation, and aftermarket-revenue durability are not yet substantiated for a buyer.
Control/timing constraint: Founder wants a defensible valuation but will not run a rushed process that signals distress to customers, competitors, or the workforce.
ownerIntake.immediateConcern: The 64-year-old founder wants liquidity and an orderly transition within ~18-24 months but has no internal successor and depends heavily on a few long-tenured people. He must choose a path: (A) sell to a financial/PE buyer (faster, more standardized process, but typically valued on EBITDA multiple and may require an earn-out or management retention he cannot personally provide), (B) sell to a strategic buyer (a larger manufacturer or channel that could pay a premium for synergies but may integrate/relocate and is harder to source), or (C) retain ownership and run for cash flow with a hired professional manager (preserves control and reputation but defers liquidity and concentrates the founder's wealth in an illiquid, key-person-dependent asset). The business's transferable value, the durability of its aftermarket stream, and the depth of its key-person dependence are not yet substantiated to buyer-diligence standard.

businessProblem: A mature, profitable $85M-revenue industrial equipment manufacturer (~$11M EBITDA, higher-margin ~30% aftermarket stream) is owned ~100% by a 64-year-old founder who wants a fair liquidity event and an orderly exit within ~18-24 months while protecting ~310 employees and a 40-year reputation. There is no internal successor and value is concentrated in the founder and 2-3 long-tenured leaders, with top-5 customer concentration at ~38%. He must choose among (A) a financial/PE buyer (faster, EBITDA-multiple-based, often requiring an earn-out or management retention he cannot personally provide), (B) a strategic buyer (potential synergy premium but integration/relocation risk and harder to source), or (C) retaining and running for cash flow with hired management (preserves control/reputation but defers liquidity and concentrates wealth in an illiquid, key-person-dependent asset). The business's transferable value, aftermarket durability, and key-person dependence are not yet substantiated to buyer-diligence standard, and any path that requires the founder's continued daily leadership past ~24 months is unacceptable.

evidence.finding: Earnings are solid but the realizable multiple hinges on diligence-readiness and earnings quality. EBITDA is ~$11M at a 13% margin with modest net debt (~$8M) and a 7-month backlog. Comps suggest ~5-7x EBITDA from financial buyers and ~7-10x from strategics for assets with durable aftermarket and clean diligence. But there is no recent quality-of-earnings study and statements are unaudited, so normalized EBITDA and the achievable multiple are not yet substantiated, leaving a wide and unverified valuation range.
evidence.source: Internal financials, comparable-transaction benchmarks, banker preliminary read

evidence.finding: The dominant transferability risk is key-person and succession dependence. There is no internal CEO successor, and senior engineering plus the top-5 customer relationships (~38% of revenue) are concentrated in the founder and 2-3 long-tenured leaders. A buyer's price and a retain-and-hire plan both depend on how much value survives the founder's exit, which is currently undocumented. This is the central driver of both the achievable multiple and the feasibility of an owner exit within 24 months.
evidence.source: Organizational review, customer-relationship mapping, succession assessment

evidence.finding: The higher-margin aftermarket stream (~30% of revenue, ~28% gross vs ~21% on machinery) is the most valuable and most scrutinized asset, but its durability is uncharacterized. It is unknown whether this stream is contracted/recurring or relationship-dependent and therefore at risk in a transition. Buyers (especially strategics paying a premium) will price the aftermarket heavily on its proven recurrence and stickiness through an ownership change.
evidence.source: Segment revenue analysis, aftermarket contract review (incomplete)

evidence.finding: Path feasibility differs sharply by buyer type and by the founder's constraints. A financial buyer offers a faster, standardized process but typically expects management continuity or an earn-out the founder cannot personally provide past 24 months, and prices on multiple. A strategic buyer could pay a synergy premium but may integrate or relocate the plant (conflicting with the workforce/reputation constraint) and is harder to source. Retaining requires hiring a credible professional manager into a key-person-dependent business and defers liquidity. None of the three can be ranked without substantiated transferable value and aftermarket durability.

supportingData.strategic_buyer: premium possible, integration/relocation risk, harder to source
supportingData.retain_run: preserves control/reputation, defers liquidity, needs hired CEO

evidence.finding: The owner's actual after-tax outcome under each path is unquantified. Multiple, structure (cash vs earn-out vs rollover equity), tax treatment, and the founder's personal liquidity needs combine differently across A, B, and C, so the option that maximizes after-tax, risk-adjusted proceeds within the founder's constraints cannot be identified from headline multiples alone.
evidence.source: Preliminary tax/structure notes, owner financial-planning gap assessment

strategicOptions.description: Run a process to sell to a financial/PE buyer at an EBITDA multiple, accepting a faster, more standardized transaction and structuring around the founder's unwillingness to provide a long earn-out (e.g., professional-management bridge, rollover, or shorter transition).
strategicOptions.rationale: Faster and more predictable liquidity at a market multiple, with a broad buyer pool. Best if normalized EBITDA is substantiated and the key-person/aftermarket risks can be mitigated enough to attract a clean multiple without a long owner commitment.
strategicOptions.implementationRisk: MEDIUM (typically expects management continuity or earn-out the founder cannot personally provide; multiple discounted if key-person dependence and aftermarket durability are not substantiated)

strategicOptions.description: Pursue a strategic buyer (larger manufacturer/channel) that could pay a synergy premium (~7-10x), accepting that integration or plant relocation may follow and that sourcing the right strategic and negotiating workforce/reputation protections takes longer.
strategicOptions.rationale: Highest potential price via synergies and the most natural owner of the aftermarket and customer base. Best if a strategic that will preserve workforce/reputation can be sourced and the aftermarket durability supports a premium.
strategicOptions.implementationRisk: MEDIUM-HIGH (integration/relocation risk conflicts with workforce/reputation constraint; harder to source; premium contingent on substantiated aftermarket and clean diligence)
strategicOptions.timelineIfChosen: 12-24 months to source, negotiate, and close

strategicOptions.description: Retain ownership and install a hired professional manager, running the business for cash flow and distributions while building succession depth, deferring a sale until transferable value and aftermarket durability are stronger (or indefinitely).
strategicOptions.rationale: Preserves control, workforce, and reputation and avoids a forced or discounted sale. Best if a credible CEO can be hired and the founder accepts deferred, concentrated, illiquid wealth.
strategicOptions.implementationRisk: HIGH (requires hiring a credible CEO into a key-person-dependent business; defers liquidity and concentrates the founder's wealth in an illiquid asset; does not satisfy the near-term liquidity goal)
strategicOptions.timelineIfChosen: Ongoing; liquidity deferred 3+ years or indefinitely
